newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil prices ease as Iraq defuses US showdown.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil prices ease as Iraq defuses US showdown.

text.p: Buoyant oil prices fell on Monday after Iraq appeared to defuse a military showdown with Washington by suspending attacks on U.S. warplanes patrolling Iraqi no fly zones.
November futures for international benchmark North Sea Brent blend traded down 70 cents at $22.43 a barrel shortly after opening in London.
Brent for October hit a five-year post Gulf War peak at $24.39 a barrel last Thursday after Iraq fired missiles at U.S. planes and Washington sent more weaponry to the region.
Traders said Baghdad's apparent decision to step back from the brink of all-out confrontation probably meant oil prices had peaked, for the time being at least.
"The shooting has stopped and that's given the market the chance to retrace some of its big gains," said Bo van Wijk at Swiss bank UBS.
"We shorted (sold) the market on Friday because we felt that it had hit a short-term top on Iraq," said a London-based oil trader at U.S. company.
But dealers warned that a resumption of military activity in the region, raising the spectre of a disruption to Middle East crude supplies, could easily send oil soaring again.

"I don't think at this stage that we'll see dramatically higher prices but Saddam is out of his cage, he appears to be ahead of the game politically and that spells danger for the market," said Russell Hill, head of trading at oil company OMV in London.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry on Sunday in Kuwait held out the possibility of further strikes against Iraq and dismissed Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's pledge to abandon attacks on U.S. air patrols.
Perry, looking to drum up support among hesitant Gulf War Arab allies, warned Saddam could move to "coerce or even attack" his neighbours to the south.
Any Iraqi move against Kuwait could send prices spiralling toward the $40 a barrel of 1990 after Baghdad's invasion.
Kuwait and Gulf neighbour Saudi Arabia contribute 10 million barrels a day (bpd) of the world's 70 million supplies.

Diplomats, however, think Saddam is unlikely to attempt a repeat given his massive military disadvantage against U.S. forces in the region. Traders said that the onset of peak winter demand at at time of low inventories in the west, would almost certainly prevent any big slump in the value of crude.
"We have very low distillate (heating oil and diesel) stocks already and its not even October," said van Wijk at UBS. "The market will remain very well supported whatever happens in Iraq."

Hard-pressed oil buyers already are having to cope without several hundred thousand barrels a day of Iraqi crude expected back on the market under an oil-for-food exchange arranged with Iraq by the United Nations in May.
The accord, designed to raise cash for humanitarian supplies in Iraq, was put on hold after Baghdad sent troops into northern Iraq's Kurdish safe havens.

"We have to remember that the Iraqi oil is unlikely to reach the market any time this year," said Alistair Harris. "With distillate stocks so low the market could quite easily have the opportunity to go higher again."
